title: Record Heat Bakes UK and Europe: Hospitals, Wildfires, and Drought
summary:
On Thursday, August 13, 2026, the UK recorded its hottest day of the year, with temperatures reaching 38.1°C (100.6°F) in west London, according to the national weather service. This marks the UK's fifth heat wave of the year, and 2026 has now seen a record four days at or above 36°C. France is even hotter, with several areas approaching 41°C (106°F).

The extreme heat is taking a toll on healthcare workers. The Royal College of Nursing reported that nurses have collapsed from heat exhaustion in hospitals, many of which are housed in aging buildings without adequate cooling. "When nursing staff are collapsing, feeling dizzy, sick or even being admitted to the very hospitals they work in because their workplaces cannot handle the heat, it shows just how badly they are being failed," said Nicola Ranger, the college's chief executive.

Drought conditions are widespread across Britain and France, shriveling crops and draining rivers. Britain's Southern Water has applied for a rare drought order that would ban businesses from nonessential water use, such as cleaning cars and filling nondomestic swimming pools. If approved by Environment Secretary Angela Eagle, it would be the first such ban since May 2006.

Wildfires are a major threat. In northern Greece, more than 300 vacationers and residents were evacuated by sea after a wildfire swept through a pine forest near the Siviri resort. In England, firefighters are battling a blaze in the New Forest, and 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year—matching last year's record. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will consider banning disposable barbecues, stating, "People should not be using those barbecues outside at this moment in time." French firefighters, exhausted after a desperate summer, are threatening to strike for more resources.
why_it_matters: Heat waves are no longer rare events; they put pressure on hospitals, water supplies, and emergency services. For your generation, adapting buildings and rules to heat—not just reacting each summer—will shape where and how safely people can live, work, and go to school as the climate continues to warm.

background_read: The UK's national weather service is the Met Office; its recorded national high stood at 40.3°C (104.5°F) in July 2022 at Coningsby in Lincolnshire, so a 38.1°C day fits the recent pattern of more frequent and intense heat.

The Royal College of Nursing is a professional body and trade union representing nurses; it campaigns on workplace safety, and its warning points to older hospital buildings that often lack air conditioning or effective cooling.

Southern Water is a private utility that supplies water and treats wastewater in parts of southern England; under UK law, a drought order is a temporary measure that can prohibit nonessential water use when supplies are badly strained.
Environment Secretary Angela Eagle is the UK minister responsible for environmental regulation; the last comparable drought order mentioned dates to May 2006, which shows how rare such bans are.

Andy Burnham, named as Prime Minister in the article, is shown responding to fire risk by considering a ban on disposable barbecues. Wildfire risk rises when vegetation dries out in heat; Mediterranean tourist areas often evacuate people by sea when fires move fast.

perspectives.description: The drought order is a preventative tool that could save water supplies if approved, and public warnings about disposable barbecues may reduce fire risk. Recording heat and fire data helps officials see when emergency services need more support.

Healthcare workers are being failed by hospitals that are too hot for staff and patients, and the Royal College of Nursing describes nurses collapsing or being admitted to their own workplaces. Firefighters in France are exhausted enough to threaten strikes, and farmers are watching crops shrivel and rivers drain.

The article shows how extreme heat creates linked problems: high temperatures strain health systems, dry conditions reduce water availability, and wildfires threaten communities. The first drought order since May 2006 is a sign that water stress is moving into emergency territory, not just a one-day weather event.

If such heat waves continue, governments may have to retrofit hospitals, update building codes, store more water, and strengthen fire services. The discussion of banning disposable barbecues may be only a first step toward more permanent rules for living with hotter summers.
